Few things of note to criticals that a lot of people miss:

Criticals ALWAYS HIT, regardless of what it is. This means that anyone, at any given point in time, can hurt something immortal with a minimum of 5% chance. Call it the power of a miracle or something.

Criticals only double dice rolls from damage (not modifiers), from any source, as long as it came from an attack. What this means is:

  • Ranged spell ATTACKS can crit.
  • Sneak attacks are doubled (it's a dice roll).
  • Smite bonuses are doubled (same as sneak attack).

Orcs can add a single damage dice from their weapon when they crit with that weapon. So if you have a 2d6, you would double that (4d6) and add one more die for a total of 5d6. Do a bit of math, and you'll realize this works the best with weapons that have fewer damage dice.

An orc with a 2d6 weapon (average 7) on a crit will do an average of 17.5 damage, but the same orc with a 1d12 (average 6.5) will do an average of 19.5.

In a similar way, the Great Weapon Fighting style with a 2d6 has a 1/3 chance of activating every hit, but on a 1d12 it's only a 1/6 chance.

And on top of that, the Savage Attacker feat increases the average damage of a single swing of a 2d6 (7 normally) to a 8.25, but increases the 1d12 (6.5 normally) to a 9.25.

All things to consider.

One thing of note, having advantage doesn't necessarily grant you double the chance to crit, more like reduces the chances of not critting.

Say you have a 90% chance to not crit. So your 10% chance to crit is really just reducing the chance to NOT crit (basically 100% if you take out crit chance).

Once again, 90% chance to not crit. Now you have advantage, and now you simply just reduce the current chance to not crit by ANOTHER 10%, but it scales with the current chance to not crit. In other words, reduce that 90 by 10% and you'll get 9. Giving a roll advantage will give you another 9% chance to crit.

Getting advantage will give you a 81% chance to not crit, or a 19% chance to crit.

With your current math, rolling the dice 10 times will always result with a 19-20, which we all know isn't true. It's not a major issue, 19% is pretty close to 20%, but you don't want to confuse the two before you start doing your math and start realizing that you SHOULD have 50% to crit but really only getting them about a third of the time.

In case you're interested for future use, advantage on a d20 basically gives about +5 to a roll, where disadvantage gives about -5.

An easy way of doing it is 1-Fd, where F is the percent chance to fail to do what you want, in 0.XX style, and 'd' is the number of dice attempts you're given.

So with a 10% chance to crit with 2 dice, that's 1-(0.92), you get 19. You originally had a 10% chance to crit with a single die, with two dice you'll have 19%. With 3 dice, it's 27%. 4 dice is 0.34%, 5 dice is 41%.

A note on the Saving Throw issue, check out Aura of Protection (Paladin feature @ 6). Gives Charisma mod to saving throws, including yourself, with a minimum bonus of 1.

On top of that, all of your smite spells DO require concentration, but they can be expended the same turn they're activated. The idea is, you use your bonus action to cast them then immediately expend them. They really only have the concentration ability to prevent players from stacking buffs on themselves and then smack something really hard.
Yeah, they're "Concentration" spells that last for less than a second, just because you're not allowed to have two concentration spells active.

Beyond your instant smite attacks, the only combat aura spell that uses concentration is obtained at level 9, so you already have the bonus on all saving throws due to Aura of Protection (which is always on as long as you're not unconscious).

Now, given, your proficiency mod will be a 3 when you get Aura of Prot and your Cha mod will probably be smaller than that, I would still consider going through Paladin, unless you really want maximum burst damage.

As for the reasons to pick up things early, here's a few solid examples of great level 1 classes to pick up:

  • Rogue (sneak attack damage AND expertise)
  • Barbarian (Rage makes you take half physical damage for one minute)
  • Almost any Cleric (Reaction Thunderwave, buff healing spells, proficiency in armor and weapons, make extra attacks with a bonus action, ALL LEVEL 1 PICKUPS)

There ARE options for early game multiclassing. Unfortunately, there's a lot of overlap between the fighter and the paladin (fighting styles, proficiency in weapons and armor) and Second Wind scales with fighter level, not constitution or anything else your paladin levels will improve.

While early game fighter IS good, even for multiclassing, I usually would only consider it for a class that needs the proficiency for armor (like the wizard), as the second wind will quickly become useless.

Action Surge IS really good, and the crit bonus will definitely help scale with your paladin. I just don't think the Fighter is all that great of a multiclass option. Probably one of the best classes to specialize in, though.
